messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eduardo worked as a tax consultant, navigating the predictable rhythms of fiscal calendars until a routine traffic stop fractured his world. The incident occurred on a poorly lit highway when an officer’s hand flew to his holster, and within seconds, the cold bite of a baton against his side gave way to the sharp sting of a knee in his back. He lay pressed against the asphalt, the metallic taste of blood in his mouth, as the harsh spotlight blinded him. That moment left him with a searing awareness of bodily harm, making any sign of physical injury instantly terrifying. In the months that followed, a dull ache settled into his right ribs whenever he sat upright at his desk, a somatic reminder that refused to fade. Walking past a grocery store, he saw a delivery driver clutching a swollen, bruised forearm. The sight of that visible wound triggered a wave of nausea so profound he had to grip the steering wheel. As the somatic pain in his ribs flared and the victim memories of the driver’s bruised arm flashed in his mind, these intrusions actively fueled his belief that there was something fundamentally flawed about him that must have caused the encounter, while simultaneously convincing him that his life had lost all value. Eduardo had come to believe that his own brokenness made him unsafe, a conviction that drove him to meticulously plan escape routes and avoid unfamiliar places entirely. He was certain that stepping into an uncharted street invited the same violence, so he began checking behind himself every time he left his house, treating each unfamiliar environment as a potential ambush. His occupation became a labyrinth of constraints. During a client review in an unfamiliar downtown tower, Eduardo spent half the meeting fixated on the service elevator versus the stairwell, his shoulders locked against his neck. Because his relentless escape route planning and constant checking behind him kept his nervous system in a state of high alert, ordinary stimuli began to dominate his attention. What frightened him most was how his own hypervigilance amplified his triggers; a flash of red on a client’s scraped knuckle or a sudden twinge in his own side would instantly hijack his focus, making the visual and somatic intrusions impossible to dismiss. His pattern of avoiding unfamiliar places and compulsively checking behind himself did not bring safety; instead, it reinforced his deepest fears. Each time he retreated from a gathering or turned down a meeting in a new district, he felt his sense of isolation deepen, and the conviction that his life was not worth living grew heavier, confirming his belief that he was inherently to blame. The recent dissolution of his marriage had removed his last tether to normalcy, leaving him alone with the mounting symptoms. The checking behaviors and escape planning that once felt like protection now acted as silent validators of his psychological collapse. Now, at fifty-three, Eduardo sits in his study late into the night, the tax forms stacked neatly but untouched on his desk. The constant calculation of exit strategies has left him exhausted, and the isolation has stretched into a quiet despair. He finally booked this intake because the weight of his own perceived fault and the belief that his days lack meaning have begun to overshadow even his physical discomfort. He is afraid that without intervention, the loop of checking and withdrawing will consume whatever remains of his professional life and his capacity for peace. At the same time, he hopes to find a way to quiet the constant alarm, to look at his own hands without bracing for impact, and to discover whether life can ever feel worth living again.
